'''Colonel Parker Hitt''' (August 27, 1878 – March 2, 1971) was a United States Army officer and a pioneer in the field of [[cryptology]]. Often cited as the "father of modern American military cryptology," Hitt authored the first practical work on military ciphers in the United States in over a century and invented foundational cryptographic devices that remained in use through [[World War II]].<ref name="NSA_Bio">{{cite web |title=Colonel Parker Hitt |url=https://www.nsa.gov/History/Cryptologic-History/Historical-Figures/Historical-Figures-View/Article/1621575/colonel-parker-hitt/ |publisher=National Security Agency/Central Security Service |access-date=2024-07-13}}</ref><ref name="Smoot_Bio">{{cite book|last=Smoot|first=Betsy Rohaly|date=2022|title=Parker Hitt: The Father of American Military Cryptology|publisher=University Press of Kentucky| isbn=978-0-8131-8240-7}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Parker Hitt was born in [[Indianapolis]], Indiana, on August 27, 1878.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /> He attended [[Purdue University]] to study civil engineering but dropped out during his senior year in 1898 to enlist for service in the [[Spanish–American War]].<ref name="Smoot_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS">{{cite web |last=Stewart |first=Lori |title=Father of American Military Cryptology Passes Away (2 MAR 1971) |url=https://www.dvidshub.net/news/491777/father-american-military-cryptology-passes-away-2-mar-1971 |publisher=DVIDS Hub |date=2025-02-28}}</ref> He served as a sergeant in the 2nd U.S. Volunteer Engineers in [[Cuba]] before being commissioned as a second lieutenant in the 22nd Infantry in 1899.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" />

== Military career ==
Hitt's early military career included postings in the [[Philippines]], [[California]], and [[Alaska]].<ref name="NSA_Bio" /> In 1911, he attended the Signal Corps School at [[Fort Leavenworth]], where his technical aptitude led to an appointment as an instructor.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Smoot_Bio" /> Between 1912 and 1915, he taught courses on codes, ciphers, and radio theory, significantly influencing the Army's communication doctrine.<ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /><ref name="Smoot_Bio" />

During the [[Pancho Villa Expedition|Punitive Expedition]] in 1916, Hitt and his wife, [[Genevieve Young Hitt]], solved intercepted Mexican government communications.<ref name="Smoot_Bio" /><ref name="Christensen_Review">{{cite journal|last1=Christensen|first1=Chris |date=2022|title=Review of Parker Hitt: The Father of American Military Cryptology by Betsy Rohaly Smoot|journal=[[Cryptologia]]|volume= 47|issue=5|pages=489–492 |doi=10.1080/01611194.2022.2101404 }}.</ref> Following the U.S. entry into [[World War I]], General [[John J. Pershing]] selected Hitt for his staff in the [[American Expeditionary Forces]] (AEF).<ref name="NSA_Bio" /> Hitt served as a Senior Signal Officer, overseeing the development of the "Radio Service Code" and supervising the coding and decoding of all AEF messages until a permanent headquarters was established in Paris.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /> He was also instrumental in the employment of American female telephone operators, popularly known as the "[[Hello Girls]]," to manage switchboards for the First Army.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Frahm_HelloGirls">Frahm, Jill (2016). "Women Telephone Operators in World War I France". ''National Cryptologic Foundation''.</ref>

Hitt retired as a colonel in 1928 but was recalled to active duty in 1940 at the age of 62.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /> During [[World War II]], he served as the Signal Officer for the Fifth Corps Area at Fort Hayes, Ohio, until his final retirement in 1944.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Christensen_Review" />

== Contributions to American cryptology ==
Hitt is credited with modernizing American cryptanalysis through his teaching and inventions. He famously stated that success in cryptanalysis relied on four factors: "perseverance, careful methods of analysis, intuition, and luck."<ref name="Hitt_Manual">{{cite book|last=Hitt|first= Parker|date=1916|title=Manual for the Solution of Military Ciphers|publisher=Army Service Schools Press}}</ref>

=== ''Manual for the Solution of Military Ciphers'' ===
In 1916, Hitt published his seminal work, ''Manual for the Solution of Military Ciphers''. It was the first practical U.S. instructional text on cryptanalysis in a century.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /> The manual provided the foundation for training American cryptologists during World War I and was cited by [[William F. Friedman]] as the work that "launched" his career in the science.<ref name="Friedman_Legacy">''The Friedman Legacy: A Tribute to William and Elizebeth Friedman'' (2006). Center for Cryptologic History, National Security Agency.</ref>

=== Inventions ===
Finding the official Army field cipher insecure, Hitt proposed mechanical alternatives:
* '''The Cylinder Cipher:''' In 1912, Hitt built a prototype cylindrical device. This design was later refined by Major [[Joseph Mauborgne]] into the [[M-94]], which the Army adopted in 1922 and used for over two decades.<ref name="Smoot_Cylinder">{{cite journal|last1=Smoot| first1=Betsy Rohaly|date=2015|title=Parker Hitt's First Cylinder Device and the Genesis of U.S. Army Cylinder and Strip Devices|journal=[[Cryptologia]]|volume=39|issue=4|pages=315–321| doi=10.1080/01611194.2014.988371}}</ref><ref name="CryptoMuseum_M94">{{cite web |title=M-94 |url=https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/usa/m94/index.htm |publisher=Crypto Museum |access-date=2024-07-13}}</ref>
* '''The Sliding Strip Cipher:''' Hitt developed a flat version of the cylinder device using alphabetic strips. This evolved into the [[M-138-A]], used extensively by the [[United States Department of State|State Department]] and [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]] during the 1930s and World War II.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Smoot_Cylinder" />

While working for [[ITT Inc.|IT&T]] in the 1930s, Hitt invented a teletypewriter cipher machine. Legally obtained details of his scrambler design were reportedly utilized by the German Lorenz Company to develop the [[Lorenz cipher|Lorenz SZ (Tunny)]] machine used by Germany in World War II.<ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /><ref name="Christensen_Review" />

== Personal life ==
In 1911, Hitt married [[Genevieve Young Hitt]]. Genevieve became the first woman to break ciphers for the U.S. government while working as a paid codebreaker for the Army's Southern Department.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="IU_Genevieve">{{cite web |title=Genevieve Young Hitt |url=https://womenandtech.indiana.edu/programs/cybersecurity/profiles-cybersecurity-women/genevieve-young-hitt.html |publisher=Indiana University Center of Excellence for Women & Technology |access-date=2024-07-13}}</ref> Their daughter, Mary Lueise Hitt, also served as a "code girl" and teleprinter operator during World War II.<ref name="Smoot_Bio" /><ref name="Christensen_Review" />

Hitt spent his final years on a farm in [[Front Royal, Virginia]], where he raised dogs. He died on March 2, 1971, at the age of 92.<ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" /> His daughter recalled his modest final words as, "I should have had more dogs."<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="Stewart_DVIDS" />

== Legacy ==
Hitt was posthumously inducted into the [[Military Intelligence Hall of Fame]] in 1988 and the [[NSA Hall of Honor|NSA/CSS Cryptologic Hall of Honor]] in 2011.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /><ref name="MIHOF">{{cite web |title=Colonel Parker Hitt, US Army, Retired (Deceased) |url=https://www.ikn.army.mil/apps/MIHOF/biographies/Hitt,%20Parker.pdf |publisher=Military Intelligence Corps Hall of Fame |access-date=2024-07-13}}</ref> '''Hitt Hall''' at [[Fort Huachuca]] was named in his honor in 1995.<ref name="NSA_Bio" /> During the 1930s, he was a key mentor to the [[American Cryptogram Association]] (ACA), providing technical advice to authors like [[Helen Fouché Gaines]].<ref name="Smoot_Bio" /><ref name="Christensen_Review" />
